$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](images/54/54dad1c9d747fead6f27dd0e9af7cca434c40a83d56c02c854bb610a1cdc6087.svg)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](images/d2/d28cf572126716928bc9ded7c2646871540e20b1d93d1efc929599b4c379d38b.svg)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124413 :question/problem "Given the matrix 
![](images/3d/3da867d461c2b42c21badd67ce59c9ec5f6448597b4d2dcbb7e8b28ffe397768.svg) 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D=P^{-1}AP.$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). So, $x_1$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_2=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](images/04/04f6efaa2bb141940040a04905e52aacd7aa739e1bd58dd71666a10543ff0f74.svg)
Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector ![](images/dd/dd78cbf2025fdf012dc27429596c84be09825b436c32a5410f50f78cd4943a66.svg)

- For $\lambda_2=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The above matrix corresponds to a homogeneous system of linear equations. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=\dfrac{8}{5}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is
![](images/5b/5b5b06d4cd243ca0370807b58bc9d0da68f34aa008956016bab3da29377df219.svg)
Setting  $x_2=5,$ we get the eigenvector  ![](images/3e/3ea698aa474cb6d28b3fb511215fbe5da7d01b6653e884719d99483eac5635a0.svg)

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:
![](images/b7/b736228d68ad58b430f707236014be76e0354bf42ff9fcd73c495a077835bad7.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

![](images/9d/9dee6d9184932a79f36305b9fca2bbb5a2a18bc79b49ad97038f780a2f125e49.svg)

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

![](images/ca/caa7716ce45eef38d92092d27827d30fd539fca27067c1e12f485a719b4f37ae.svg)

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

![](images/3e/3e0df792d822773528cb07cceb39fcb98b7397ae70ab4f114e1450f1d91256d1.svg)

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

![](images/86/869a05b6273dbbb1b53d9f842d8b2c612017517a0b007c1c5f494f55439a11b4.svg)

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

*If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have
![](images/e1/e1468bc5ccdff43e33587c7b4b500bc527ab0ac7e74410ea53df1f803a19b520.svg)

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace $V_\lambda$ must be of dimension $2.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125842 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

![](images/76/76843143729d2bc62fc74dc6f03c24eb6a12dfc16a2609a8f2b36499cf39ce90.svg)

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

![](images/de/dec5fece3d89eaa022b4e951e63259b0f87213997397b1f8a91fb8fdabed0f74.svg)

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124753 :activity/expected-seconds 1080.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

Given that $D=P^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\dfrac{a}{b}.$" :question/worked-solution "From the diagonal matrix ![](images/f3/f3460b47901f79529216c1440403e2115ff9047cb997070893b241cd938728de.png) we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get  

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). So, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1= -{2}x_2.$ Therefore, the general solution is

![](images/95/95d1bcb284138711bcf5afddb3f09c702e664fbdc7b256b0eaf81044f87403cf.png)

By setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](images/89/898d72a1a0cc123d1ff7ecb4c8d02f6951739a9498e36ff14ee44cb322952fb6.png)

Finally, $\dfrac{a}{b}=\dfrac{-2}{1} = -2.$"} {:db/id 17592186125019 :question/id #uuid "47e69096-fce9-5678-91d0-dfdd65324d6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36908"} {:db/id 17592186125030 :question/id {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}∗ & 1 \\ ∗ & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$   find the first column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$  

So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].$"} {:db/id 17592186348385 :question/id #uuid "4f9c3543-a306-5635-8fa9-149cba24aebf" :question/math-academy-id "q-80457"} {:db/id So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -8 \\ 4 & -5\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\lambda_1=3, \quad\quad\lambda_2=-2.
$$

$$

$$

To solve the corresponding system of linear equations, we construct the augmented matrix $M$ and reduce it to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}={R}_{2}+(-\frac{5}{8}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$

-8\end{aligned}].$" :question/worked-solution "We apply the diagonalization algorithm. 

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $E$ using its characteristic equation $det(E-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & 9 \\ -6 & -8-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-8-\lambda )-9\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $E$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $E.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=-2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}E-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 9 \\ -6 & -8\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 \\ -6 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ -6 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{2}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ and

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 15\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.
$$

[{:db/id 17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125539 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125840 :tutorial/content "There is a theorem that states the following:

> *If $A$ is a $2 \times 2$ matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A.$*

We can break this down into two possible cases:

- If $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue). 

So, for a matrix $A$ with eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ and corresponding eigenvectors $\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2},$ we have

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

- If we get a double root $\lambda$ of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable *only if* we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda,$ which may or may not be possible. $$
A=PDP^{-1}.
$$

 

We can write this equation in an equivalent form, making $D$ the subject.

First, we left-multiply both sides of the equation by $P^{-1}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}\cdot A & ={P}^{-1}\cdot PD{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & ={I}_{2}D{P}^{-1} \\ {P}^{-1}A & =D{P}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we right-multiply both sides of the equation by $P{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1}A\cdot P & =D{P}^{-1}\cdot P \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D{I}_{2} \\ {P}^{-1}AP & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
A=PDP^{-1}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
D = P^{-1}A P.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6e0a81c7-a393-5e5d-b8c1-16d982404f1a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5085 :tutorial/title "The Connection Between a Matrix and Its Diagonal Form"} :step/id #uuid :step/content {:db/id 17592186125842 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization 

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{2} & {v}_{1} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "eb055132-9c7d-55a5-a2c6-0bcb54877c1c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5086 :tutorial/title "Uniqueness of the Diagonalization"} :step/id #uuid "a11b9aec-3c2f-5a01-8b7c-600351ec33e2" :step/math-academy-id 31854 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125662}} {:db/id 17592186125662 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125896 :tutorial/content "Let ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) be a diagonalizable ![](images/25/2521651122403a440e682fef383af333958f5b0d1334abe8b0771865d4daf100.svg) matrix. ![](images/14/1459b0643f99c186f9710118617f89f34a601526e7154213471404d2feb2aaeb.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "61524e43-2735-5e5a-904b-2c4973df94a9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7958 :tutorial/title "Diagonalization as a Change of Coordinates"} :step/id #uuid "831d0bbd-aa17-5012-9d8b-073e0d2d67a6" :step/math-academy-id 45769}] :activity/title "Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124753} {:db/id 17592186125538 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
A = PDP^{-1}.
$$

So, to **diagonalize** a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ that satisfy the equation above.

For example, let's diagonalize the matrix $A,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

To diagonalize a $2\times 2$ matrix, we follow a three-step **diagonalization algorithm.**

**Step 1:** Find the eigenvalues of the matrix.

We solve the characteristic equation $\vert A - \lambda I \vert = 0.$ For the given matrix, the eigenvalues are $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3.$

**Step 2:** Find a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of the matrix.

Following the usual method for computing eigenvectors, we get 

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

corresponding to the eigenvalues $\color{red}\lambda_1 =2$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2 =3,$ respectively.

Note that $\left\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{v_1}}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}\right\}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ since eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent. This becomes important later.

**Step 3: ** Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

Now that we have our eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors, we can construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and invertible matrix $P.$

The matrix $D$ has the eigenvalues of the matrix as its entries on the diagonal. For now, we can write them in any order. So, we let

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Then, the columns of $P$ are the corresponding eigenvectors. We need to write each eigenvector in the *same* column as its respective eigenvalue in the matrix $D.$ So, we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A=PD{P}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can check our solution by computing the product on the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1f56a4e0-1c9c-573c-95a9-92a93682f0a2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5083 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0dec286b-a54f-500f-b0be-886c4e33f4ba" :step/math-academy-id 31836 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125544}} {:db/id 17592186125839 :tutorial/content "A square matrix $A$ is called **diagonalizable** if there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix $D,$ we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in $D,$ we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in $P{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{2} & {v}_{1} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]
$$

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$ can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix $P$ is unique up to multiples of its columns." :tutorial/id #uuid "eb055132-9c7d-55a5-a2c6-0bcb54877c1c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5086 :tutorial/title "Uniqueness of the Diagonalization"} :step/id #uuid "a11b9aec-3c2f-5a01-8b7c-600351ec33e2" :step/math-academy-id 31854 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125662}} {:db/id 17592186125842 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ the diagonalization
